title: Two Phones, One Alert Check: Make Sure Warnings Can Reach You
subtitle: A calm, practical review can help partners distinguish phone-based emergency alerts from local services that require a separate sign-up—and make sure each person knows what their own device is set to receive.

body: Warnings are a household communication tool

Phones are often treated as if they all receive the same warnings in the same way. In practice, a useful household check starts by separating two channels: Wireless Emergency Alerts, or WEA, sent to compatible phones in an affected area, and local alert services—such as a town or county text or email program—that may require a person to register. They serve different routes to information, and one does not automatically stand in for the other. [1]

That distinction matters for couples, housemates and families who assume that one person’s phone settings, account or sign-up covers everybody. A short conversation can replace that guesswork with a clear record: which alerts each person’s phone is set to receive, whether a local service needs enrollment, and where to check the current instructions.
Start with each person’s own phone

Choose a few unhurried minutes when both phones are available and neither person needs to leave. Each person should navigate their own device and make their own decisions; the point is not to take over somebody else’s settings or inspect private messages. Together, agree on the goal: locate the emergency-alert controls, note what is enabled, and identify any separate local alert sign-up worth checking.

Menu names and locations can vary by device, software version, region and wireless provider. On an iPhone in the United States, Apple’s instructions direct users to Settings, then Notifications, and the Government Alerts area; the available options depend on region and supported network providers. If the menu differs, use the current instructions for that specific phone rather than relying on a remembered path. [3]

For Android and other devices, look for the emergency-alert settings using the manufacturer’s current support guidance, or ask the wireless provider where to find them. Do not assume two phones from the same household have identical options. Make a note of each person’s device type and the support page or provider contact that helped resolve any uncertainty.
Know what the phone channel can—and cannot—tell you

WEA is a government alerting channel that can send geographically targeted messages to compatible phones. FEMA says WEA messages go to equipped mobile devices within range of cell towers broadcasting in the affected area, and directs users to contact their cellular service provider to check whether a device can receive WEA. [1] The practical takeaway is not that a phone will always receive every warning, but that its settings and service are worth understanding.

A local opt-in program is different. A town, county or other local authority may offer texts, calls or email for information relevant to its area, and residents may need to enroll separately. FEMA’s guide explains that many local text and email alert systems are opt-in and recommends checking with local emergency-management or public-safety offices to find out what alerts are available in your area. [1] Search the official website for the town, county or tribal government where you live; if you are unsure which agency runs the program, ask the local emergency-management office.

If you have recently moved, changed phone numbers or changed providers, revisit the local-service question. A sign-up tied to an old address or number may not reflect where you live now. Record the official enrollment page or phone number, not just the name of a service.
Keep test alerts separate from real alerts

One small setting can cause unnecessary confusion: a phone may offer an option for test alerts. That control is not the same as the setting for actual emergency alerts. FEMA says phones ship with test alerts disabled, users must enable that option to receive WEA tests, and some phones lack a test option and cannot receive tests. [2]

During the check, read the label carefully and avoid changing a setting simply because it sounds related. If someone wants to receive test messages, they can decide that for their own device; if they do not, that choice should not be mistaken for switching off real emergency alerts. When the wording is unclear, pause and consult the phone maker’s instructions or wireless provider. The aim is to understand the controls, not to toggle through them quickly.

This distinction also helps explain why a household might not have noticed a test while still having real-alert settings enabled. Conversely, seeing a test at some point is not proof that every relevant setting, local sign-up or other way of receiving information is in place.
Make the check useful for both people

A shared review should account for how each person actually uses a phone. Someone who keeps a device on silent, relies on captions, uses a hearing aid or has visual-access needs may want to explore the alert options and accessibility features available on that specific device. Do not assume that one alert sound, vibration or display works equally well for both people. If a setting is unfamiliar, look up the current manufacturer guidance together; if the need is not met, ask the provider what options are available.

Keep the comparison simple. For each person, note the phone or device, where its alert controls are found, whether government alerts are enabled, and any question still to resolve. Then add the local service: whether it exists, who runs it, whether enrollment is needed, and where the official instructions live. Avoid writing down account passwords or placing sensitive information in a note that others can access.
A small record beats a confident guess

Write down only what will help you repeat the check. A shared note might say: “Alex: iPhone; government alert options checked; county text program still to verify.” “Sam: Android; settings located using manufacturer instructions; local email option registered.” Keep each person’s information accurate and let them choose whether the note is shared. If a phone is replaced or a number changes, the record becomes a prompt to check again rather than a permanent assurance.

A phone alert review is one layer of household readiness, not a complete plan. The signal may not reach a device for reasons outside a household’s control, and local systems have their own coverage and enrollment rules. Keep other trusted ways of receiving information in view, including official local sources. If one partner is often away from home, travels between jurisdictions or does not carry a phone consistently, discuss what information source makes sense in those situations without assuming a single fix fits everyone.
End with a clear handoff, not a promise

Before putting the phones away, each person should be able to show where their own alert settings are and say what remains uncertain. Agree who, if anyone, will look up the official local sign-up page, and where you will keep that link. If one device’s instructions are confusing, write down the exact question for its manufacturer or wireless provider instead of guessing.

Then leave the note open to revision. A checked box means you found and reviewed a setting; it does not guarantee that every warning will arrive, or that the same options will be available forever. Treat the exercise as a way to replace assumptions with a clearer picture of the channels you use. The next time someone changes phones, moves, or updates a number, you will know which parts of that picture are worth checking again.
Leave the check with one honest next move

Try this together at a kitchen table, with both phones in hand and the owners leading their own screens. Give each person a few minutes to find the alert controls and say what they can confirm; write down only the device, the location of the settings and any unresolved question. Then look up whether your town or county runs a separate opt-in service, using its official website. Finish by choosing one next step—perhaps enrolling, checking a provider’s guidance or simply saving the official page. Keep the record modest and private. It should help you find the next answer, not suggest that warnings are guaranteed.
